alternative: Give the state an owner: build it once (let state = Arc::new(Mutex::new(State::new()));) and pass clones of that handle into every value that needs it (struct Ctx { state: Arc<Mutex<State>> }), or thread a &mut State through the call graph - Rust's ownership and Send/Sync checking then makes the sharing explicit and testable. Reserve static Mutex/OnceLock/LazyLock for genuinely process-wide state that cannot be threaded through, such as a default logger.
idiom_name: static Mutex/OnceLock state behind methods on a zero-sized struct (against Rust's ownership model)
implementation_notes: Rust's statics are shared by definition but must be Sync, so a mutable monostate has to wrap the state in interior mutability - static STATE: Mutex<State> = Mutex::new(...) (const constructor since Rust 1.63) or OnceLock/LazyLock for lazy initialization - and methods on a zero-sized struct then lock on every access. What replaces the classic structure is ownership: the compiler refuses safe global mutable state, taking a reference to a static mut is deny-by-default in edition 2024, and the edition guide's advice is to avoid mutable globals and use Mutex/RwLock/OnceLock/LazyLock only when there is no alternative. The explicit form - one state value created once and shared through clones of an Arc<Mutex<_>> - keeps the pattern's behaviour (all handles observe the same data) while making the sharing visible in types; prefer it, and treat a process-global as a last resort.
pitfalls: static mut is effectively unusable: static_mut_refs is deny-by-default in edition 2024 (it was always undefined behaviour when aliased), so mutable globals must go through interior mutability.
OnceLock::get_or_init deadlocks/panics on reentrant initialization, and a panicking initializer poisons a LazyLock permanently - every later access panics.
A global mutex is still a global: tests in one process share it, and a panic while the lock is held poisons the Mutex unless PoisonError is handled.
Static state must be Sync + 'static, so non-Send types (Rc, RefCell) cannot appear in it, and locks held across await points make async code block the executor.
